content: Bronchiolitis is a severe respiratory illness that primarily affects infants and can be life-threatening. It is most commonly caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Current guidelines do not recommend the use of antibiotics for bronchiolitis unless there is a concern for complications such as secondary bacterial pneumonia or respiratory failure. Despite this, antibiotics are frequently prescribed in clinical practice. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of antibiotics in treating bronchiolitis in children under two years of age, compared to placebo or other interventions. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared antibiotics to placebo in children under two years diagnosed with bronchiolitis based on clinical criteria, such as respiratory distress following cold-like symptoms, with or without fever. The primary outcomes assessed were the time to resolution of symptoms, including respiratory distress, wheezing, crackles, oxygen saturation, and fever. Secondary outcomes included hospital admissions, length of hospital stay, readmissions, complications, adverse events, and radiological findings. The review included seven studies with a total of 824 participants. The results of these studies were often inconsistent, which limited the ability to perform a meta-analysis, except for outcomes such as mortality, duration of supplemental oxygen use, and length of hospital stay. Two new studies (281 participants) were added in this update, both of which compared azithromycin to placebo. These studies found no significant differences in the length of hospital stay, duration of oxygen requirement, or readmission rates. Similarly, an older study with 52 participants comparing ampicillin to placebo also found no significant differences in the duration of illness. One small study with 21 participants, which had a higher risk of bias, randomized children with confirmed RSV infection to receive either clarithromycin or placebo. This study suggested a potential trend toward reduced hospital readmissions with clarithromycin, but the evidence was not robust. Three studies that provided adequate data on the duration of supplemental oxygen use showed no significant difference between antibiotics and placebo (pooled mean difference: -0.20 days; 95% confidence interval: -0.72 to 0.33). Similarly, three studies that provided data on the length of hospital stay also showed no significant difference between antibiotics (azithromycin) and placebo (pooled mean difference: -0.58 days; 95% confidence interval: -1.18 to 0.02). Two studies that randomized children to receive intravenous ampicillin, oral erythromycin, or no antibiotics found no significant differences in most symptom measures. Importantly, no deaths were reported in any of the study arms, and no other adverse effects were noted. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of antibiotics for bronchiolitis in children under two years of age. However, further research may be warranted to identify specific subgroups of patients who might benefit from antibiotic therapy. Future studies should also focus on understanding why clinicians frequently prescribe antibiotics for bronchiolitis, strategies to reduce unnecessary antibiotic use, and ways to alleviate clinician anxiety about withholding antibiotics in these cases.
